sections.title: Present Tense: Three Verb Groups
sections.rule: Italian verbs fall into three groups by infinitive ending: -are, -ere, -ire. Drop the ending and add the present-tense endings. Essere (to be) and avere (to have) are irregular and essential from day one.
sections.example_target: Io parlo italiano e tu prendi un caffè.
sections.example_target_2: Lei è italiana e ha due figli.
sections.example_ref: English: I speak Italian and you have a coffee. / She is Italian and has two children.
sections.note: -are: -o/-i/-a/-iamo/-ate/-ano; -ere: -o/-i/-e/-iamo/-ete/-ono; -ire: -o/-i/-e/-iamo/-ite/-ono. Some -ire verbs add -isc- (io capisco, io finisco).

sections.title: Passato Prossimo
sections.rule: The main spoken past tense. Form it with the present of avere or essere plus the past participle: -are becomes -ato, -ere becomes -uto, -ire becomes -ito.
sections.example_target: Ho mangiato una pizza ieri sera.
sections.example_ref: English: I ate a pizza last night. / We finished the work.
sections.note: Many common verbs have irregular participles: fare->fatto, dire->detto, prendere->preso, vedere->visto, essere->stato.

sections.title: Essere vs Avere as Auxiliary
sections.rule: In compound tenses, transitive verbs and most others take avere. Verbs of motion and change of state take essere, and their participle agrees with the subject in gender and number.
sections.example_target: Sono andata al mercato.
sections.example_ref: English: I went to the market (female speaker). / I bought the bread.
sections.note: Essere verbs include andare, venire, arrivare, partire, uscire, nascere, morire, stare, restare, diventare, and all reflexive verbs.

sections.title: Imperfetto
sections.rule: The imperfetto describes habitual, ongoing, or background actions in the past ('was doing', 'used to'). Add -avo/-evo/-ivo endings to the stem; it is highly regular.
sections.example_target: Da bambino giocavo sempre a calcio.
sections.example_ref: English: As a child I always played football. / While I was reading, it was raining.
sections.note: Only a few irregulars: essere->ero, fare->facevo, dire->dicevo, bere->bevevo. Use passato prossimo for single completed actions.

sections.title: Reflexive Verbs
sections.rule: Reflexive pronouns mi/ti/si/ci/vi/si come before the verb. In the passato prossimo, reflexive verbs take essere and the participle agrees with the subject.
sections.example_target: Mi sveglio alle sette ogni mattina.
sections.example_ref: English: I wake up at seven every morning. / We had a lot of fun.
sections.note: Reflexive infinitives end in -si: lavarsi, alzarsi, chiamarsi. 'Mi chiamo Marco' means 'My name is Marco'.

sections.title: Ci and Ne
sections.rule: Ci means 'there' or 'it' (replacing a place or a + thing). Ne means 'of it/of them/some' (replacing di + thing or a quantity). Both sit directly before the verb.
sections.example_target: Vado a Roma domani. Ci vado anch'io.
sections.example_target_2: Quanti caffè bevi? Ne bevo tre.
sections.example_ref: English: I'm going to Rome tomorrow. I'm going there too. / How many coffees do you drink? I drink three of them.
sections.note: C'è = there is, ci sono = there are. 'Ne parla sempre' = he always talks about it.

sections.title: Formal Address with Lei
sections.rule: To be polite with strangers, elders, or in professional settings, use Lei with the third-person singular verb, regardless of the person's gender. Informal situations use tu with the second person.
sections.example_target: Buongiorno, come sta?
sections.example_ref: English: Good morning, how are you? (formal) / Excuse me, do you speak English? (formal)
sections.note: Informal equivalent is 'Come stai?'. Use scusi (formal) vs scusa (informal). 'Possiamo darci del tu?' politely proposes switching to informal.

sections.title: Congiuntivo Presente
sections.rule: The present subjunctive expresses doubt, wish, emotion, or opinion after che. Endings: -are verbs take -i, -ere and -ire take -a (io/tu/lui share the same form): che io parli, che io prenda, che io senta.
sections.example_target: Penso che sia una buona idea.
sections.example_target_2: Voglio che tu venga con me.
sections.example_ref: English: I think it's a good idea. / I want you to come with me.
sections.note: Key irregulars: essere->sia, avere->abbia, fare->faccia, andare->vada, potere->possa. Triggered by penso che, spero che, è importante che, benché.

sections.title: Futuro Semplice
sections.rule: The future is built from the infinitive: -are and -ere give -erò, -ire gives -irò. Endings: -ò/-ai/-à/-emo/-ete/-anno. Word stress falls on the ending.
sections.example_target: Domani partirò per Milano.
sections.example_ref: English: Tomorrow I'll leave for Milan. / Next year we'll buy a house.
sections.note: Irregular stems: essere->sarò, avere->avrò, fare->farò, andare->andrò, potere->potrò, volere->vorrò. Also used for probability: 'Sarà stanco' = He must be tired.

sections.title: Condizionale Presente
sections.rule: The conditional ('would') uses the future stem plus the endings -ei/-esti/-ebbe/-emmo/-este/-ebbero. Use it for politeness, wishes, and hypotheticals.
sections.example_target: Vorrei un caffè, per favore.
sections.example_ref: English: I would like a coffee, please. / Could you help me?
sections.note: Same irregular stems as the future: sarei, avrei, farei, andrei, potrei, vorrei. 'Mi piacerebbe' = I would like.

sections.title: Combined Object Pronouns
sections.rule: When an indirect and a direct pronoun combine, the indirect comes first and mi/ti/ci/vi change to me/te/ce/ve. Both gli and le become glie- and fuse with the direct pronoun: glielo, gliela.
sections.example_target: Me lo dai?
sections.example_target_2: Ho comprato un regalo a Maria; gliel'ho dato ieri.
sections.example_ref: English: Will you give it to me? / I bought Maria a gift; I gave it to her yesterday.
sections.note: Order: me/te/glie/ce/ve + lo/la/li/le/ne. Glielo covers both 'to him' and 'to her'.

sections.title: Imperativo
sections.rule: Informal commands: for tu, -are verbs end in -a (parla!), -ere and -ire in -i (prendi!, finisci!). The negative tu form is non + infinitive (non parlare!). The formal Lei command uses the subjunctive (parli!, prenda!).
sections.example_target: Mangia la verdura!
sections.example_ref: English: Eat your vegetables! / Don't worry!
sections.note: Pronouns attach to informal forms: dimmi! (tell me), fallo! (do it), alzati! (get up); but they precede the formal form: mi dica.

sections.title: Comparatives and Superlatives
sections.rule: Use più (more) or meno (less) before the adjective, then di before a noun or pronoun, or che when comparing two adjectives or after a preposition. The relative superlative is il/la più + adjective + di.
sections.example_target: Marco è più alto di me.
sections.example_target_2: È il ristorante più caro della città.
sections.example_ref: English: Marco is taller than me. / It's the most expensive restaurant in the city.
sections.note: Irregulars: buono->migliore, cattivo->peggiore, grande->maggiore, piccolo->minore. Use 'che' for two qualities: più intelligente che simpatico.

sections.title: Passato Remoto
sections.rule: A literary and formal past tense for completed actions, common in writing and in southern Italy. Regular forms: parlare->parlai/parlò, credere->credei/credette, finire->finii/finì.
sections.example_target: Dante scrisse la Divina Commedia.
sections.example_ref: English: Dante wrote the Divine Comedy. / He was born in Florence in 1265.
sections.note: Many irregulars: essere->fui, avere->ebbi, fare->feci, dire->dissi, vedere->vidi. In everyday speech most northern Italians use the passato prossimo instead.

sections.title: Stare plus Gerundio
sections.rule: The present progressive is stare (conjugated) plus the gerund: -are gives -ando, -ere and -ire give -endo. It stresses an action happening right now.
sections.example_target: Sto mangiando, ti richiamo dopo.
sections.example_ref: English: I'm eating, I'll call you back later. / What are you doing?
sections.note: Irregular gerunds: fare->facendo, dire->dicendo, bere->bevendo. Italian uses the simple present far more than English uses the progressive.

sections.title: Relative Pronouns
sections.rule: Che means 'who/which/that' as subject or object and never changes form. After a preposition, use cui (in cui, di cui, a cui). Il/la quale is a more formal alternative.
sections.example_target: La ragazza che parla è mia sorella.
sections.example_target_2: La città in cui vivo è piccola.
sections.example_ref: English: The girl who is speaking is my sister. / The city in which I live is small.
sections.note: 'Il cui / la cui' means 'whose' (la donna il cui marito...). Never use 'che' after a preposition; use 'cui'.

sections.title: The Partitive
sections.rule: To say 'some' or 'any', combine di with the definite article: del, dello, della, dei, degli, delle. Alternatives are un po' di, qualche + singular, and alcuni/alcune + plural.
sections.example_target: Vorrei del pane e della frutta.
sections.example_ref: English: I'd like some bread and some fruit. / I bought some flowers.
sections.note: Ne can replace the partitive: 'Ne voglio un po'' (I want some of it). In negatives the partitive is usually dropped: 'Non ho pane'.

sections.title: Trapassato Prossimo
sections.rule: The past perfect uses the imperfetto of avere or essere plus the past participle. It marks an action completed before another past action.
sections.example_target: Quando sono arrivato, il treno era già partito.
sections.example_target_2: Avevo studiato molto, così ho superato l'esame.
sections.example_ref: English: When I arrived, the train had already left. / I had studied a lot, so I passed the exam.
sections.note: The auxiliary follows the same essere/avere rules; with essere the participle agrees with the subject (era partita).

sections.title: Passive Voice
sections.rule: The passive is essere (or venire) plus the past participle, which agrees with the subject. Venire emphasizes the action, essere the resulting state. The agent is introduced by da.
sections.example_target: Il libro è stato scritto nel 1990.
sections.example_target_2: Questi prodotti vengono venduti in tutto il mondo.
sections.example_ref: English: The book was written in 1990. / These products are sold all over the world.
sections.note: The 'si passivante' is common for general statements: 'Si parla italiano' (Italian is spoken), 'Si vendono case' (houses are sold).

sections.title: Congiuntivo Imperfetto
sections.rule: The imperfect subjunctive endings are -ssi/-ssi/-sse/-ssimo/-ste/-ssero: parlassi, prendessi, finissi. Use it after past-tense triggers and in hypothetical clauses.
sections.example_target: Pensavo che fosse più facile.
sections.example_target_2: Se avessi tempo, verrei con te.
sections.example_ref: English: I thought it was easier. / If I had time, I'd come with you.
sections.note: Irregulars: essere->fossi, avere->avessi, fare->facessi, dire->dicessi, dare->dessi, stare->stessi.

sections.title: Periodo Ipotetico (If-Clauses)
sections.rule: Three types of conditionals. Reality: se + present + present/future. Possibility: se + congiuntivo imperfetto + condizionale. Impossibility (past): se + congiuntivo trapassato + condizionale composto.
sections.example_target: Se avessi tempo, verrei.
sections.example_target_2: Se avessi avuto tempo, sarei venuto.
sections.example_ref: English: If I had time, I would come. / If I had had time, I would have come.
sections.note: After 'se', never use the present conditional or present subjunctive; use the imperfect or pluperfect subjunctive.

sections.title: Condizionale Composto
sections.rule: The past conditional is the condizionale of avere or essere plus the past participle. It expresses an unrealized past ('would have') and the future-in-the-past ('was going to').
sections.example_target: Avrei voluto aiutarti, ma non ho potuto.
sections.example_ref: English: I would have liked to help you, but I couldn't. / He said he would come.
sections.note: Unlike English and French, Italian uses the past conditional (not the present) for reported future: 'Sapevo che sarebbe arrivato tardi'.
